title: The Interior of the fourth floor walk-up
premise: Astrid Okonkwo has spent six years mailing postcards to her late mother's apartment—a fourth-floor walk-up that burned down the year before her mother's death—cataloguing in them every confession she never made aloud. When a stranger named Elias Vann appears at her father's funeral calling the family by their pre-emigration name, Okonkwo-Achebe, Astrid discovers he was the fire investigator who falsified his report to protect someone he loved. To stop the sale of the ruined building and force the truth into the open, Astrid and Elias must return together to the charred walk-up, where the inventory of unsaid things finally gets spoken—and where justice arrives not through courts or inheritance law, but through testimony, restitution, and Astrid's decision to mail one last postcard with a return address.
about_author: Ulyana Brightwater is the pen name of a former probate clerk who spent a decade reading other people's unfinished letters. She writes literary fiction about the bureaucratic afterlives of love and lives above a defunct post office.

chapters.title: Return to Sender
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. At her father's sparsely attended funeral, Astrid mentally composes the week's postcard while relatives discuss the pending sale of the burned walk-up. A quiet stranger lingers at the graveside and says the family name nobody has used since Lagos: Achebe. Emotional beat: grief interrupted by recognition—the first crack in her careful system of unsaid things.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She confronts Elias outside the reception; he admits he knew her mother, Chiamaka, but refuses to say how. That night Astrid rereads her postcard archive, revealing her guilt over the night of the fire and her brother Daniel's silence since. Emotional beat: dread—her private ledger may not be as secret as she believed.

chapters.title: What the Report Said
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Flashback-weighted chapter: Elias, then a young fire investigator, ruled the fourth-floor blaze accidental despite evidence of an accelerant, because the alternative implicated the woman he loved. Present-day Elias, now dying of illness, wants to correct the record before the estate closes forever. Emotional beat: shame sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Probate and Other Small Violence
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The family meets with the estate lawyer; Daniel pushes to sell quickly, and Astrid realizes the sale will legally seal the building—and whatever evidence remains inside. She stalls the closing by contesting the will on a technicality she barely understands. Emotional beat: love against duty, as she weaponizes inheritance law against her own family's wishes.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Signed Chiamaka
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias tracks down Ngozi, the neighbor whose statement he buried years ago, and finds her keeping Chiamaka's salvaged belongings in storage. Ngozi agrees to testify only if Astrid hears it too. Emotional beat: reluctant alliance; the past acquires witnesses.

chapters.title: Fourth Floor, No Elevator
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Astrid and Elias climb the condemned stairwell of the walk-up at dawn, past water-stained walls, to the sealed unit. Among the soot they find Chiamaka's hidden letters—letters Astrid never received, addressed to her, explaining why she stayed away. Emotional beat: devastation and tenderness entwined; the mother's voice returns from ash.

chapters.title: Accelerant
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The letters reveal the truth: Daniel set the fire to destroy Chiamaka's debts and documents tied to a predatory lender, believing it would free the family; their mother died returning for Astrid's passport. Astrid must choose between protecting her brother and honoring the dead. Emotional beat: the climax of moral crisis—justice versus blood.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV. Confronted in the gutted kitchen, Daniel confesses without being asked, having carried the same inventory of unsaid things. He insists on signing a sworn statement himself, refusing Elias's offer to keep shielding him. Emotional beat: catharsis through surrender; duty finally bends toward truth.

chapters.title: Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias submits his corrected report and his own confession of falsification, accepting professional ruin and possible charges. The sale collapses; the building is designated for community land trust instead of demolition. Emotional beat: costly, unglamorous justice—no absolution, only accounting.

chapters.title: One Last Postcard
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Months later, Astrid mails a final postcard to the old address—but this time with a return address, addressed to her mother, telling her everything, including that she forgives neither easily nor fully. She and Elias stand in the walk-up's restored stairwell as new tenants move in below. Emotional beat: resolution as continuation—love outlasting duty, memory given somewhere to live.
